subject: Architecture
title: Bauhaus: The School That Built the Future
description: A 60-second lesson on Bauhaus: The School That Built the Future.

hook.text: A tiny German school lasted only 14 years. It changed how the entire world builds.

buildup.text: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in 1919, merging art, craft, and technology into one curriculum.

discovery.text: Students learned weaving, metalwork, and painting before touching architecture. Form followed function.

twist.text: The Nazis shut it down in 1933. Its teachers fled to America and spread Bauhaus ideas worldwide.

climax.text: IKEA, Apple, and every minimalist brand owe a debt to Bauhaus design principles.

punchline.text: 14 years. One school. Every modern object you own is its legacy.

quiz.question: Why did the Bauhaus school close in 1933?
options: It ran out of funding from private donors
The Nazi regime shut it down as degenerate
A fire destroyed the main campus building

details.summary: The Bauhaus school in Germany (1919–1933) unified art, craft, and technology to create a new design philosophy. Its principles — form follows function, truth to materials, and geometric simplicity — became the foundation of modern architecture and design worldwide.
details.whyItMatters: Bauhaus invented the visual language of modernity. From furniture to fonts to buildings, its ideas shaped the 20th century's built environment and continue to influence minimalist design today.
takeaways: Bauhaus unified art, craft, and technology in Germany, 1919 to 1933
Form follows function became its guiding principle
Its influence shapes modern architecture and design globally

faq.question: Why was the Bauhaus closed?
faq.answer: The Nazis shut it down in 1933, viewing its internationalist, avant-garde approach as degenerate. Many teachers — Gropius, Mies van der Rohe, Moholy-Nagy — fled to the United States, where they spread Bauhaus ideas to American architecture schools and practices.

faq.question: What did Bauhaus buildings actually look like?
faq.answer: Flat roofs, white walls, large glass curtain walls, asymmetrical compositions, and no applied ornament. The Bauhaus building in Dessau, designed by Gropius, is the definitive example — a glass-and-concrete machine for education that looks startlingly modern nearly a century later.
